stumbles.quote: Remex's hash cells hold 70% while scanning 34%.
stumbles.why: "Remex" is never explained (a library? the author's earlier system?). "Hash cells" is also undefined, so the baseline is unclear.
Refers to earlier work by the author and Oskar that the text never describes. Oskar is also never introduced.
Remex's quantization is assumed known. It is unclear what is quantized or how, and it is unclear what the baseline recall of 0.840 refers to.
The method is never defined beyond an arXiv ID. The reader can't tell how it differs from Lloyd's k-means, or what "passes" means compared with iterations.

stumbles.quote: I had expected this result to be a side note.
stumbles.why: The text does not say what the expected main result was until later. "This result" is ambiguous, and the section title and opening claim don't set it up.

stumbles.quote: the centroid table costs 126 bytes per vector
stumbles.why: The figure is unexplained. 4,096 centroids × the dimension × bytes, divided by 100,000 vectors, gives 126 only for a specific dimension and precision (768 dimensions at 4 bytes gives about 126), but none of these is stated. The reader can't check it.

stumbles.quote: A second bit per dimension would cost less than that.
stumbles.why: The comparison is implicit. It is unclear whether 2-bit quantization would achieve equal recall, and the conclusion is left unstated. It also relies on the unstated dimension.

stumbles.quote: Lloyd and e-means centroids give the same recall within 0.005, so the choice between them comes down to training time.
stumbles.why: It is unclear which recall this refers to (index-cell recall or residual-coding recall). It also sits oddly with the heading that says the centroids work best as index cells.

stumbles.quote: Used as index cells, 4,096 e-means centroids hold 90% of true neighbours while scanning 0.56% of the corpus.
stumbles.why: The probe setup is not given: how many cells are probed, at what k, and on what corpus size. 0.56% of 4,096 cells is about 23 cells' worth only if cells are equal-sized, which isn't stated.

point: E-means centroids are better used as index cells (90% recall at 0.56% scanned) than as residual-coding anchors or as a training-speed win, and they match Lloyd's recall.
